questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: The commonest direction of shoulder dislocation is:
questions.concept: Over 95% are anterior, from abduction and external rotation, giving a flattened deltoid contour with the arm held abducted. The axillary nerve must be tested for sensation over the regimental badge area before and after reduction.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Posterior shoulder dislocation is classically associated with:
questions.concept: Violent internal rotator contraction during a seizure or shock drives the head posteriorly. It is frequently missed on an anteroposterior film, showing a light-bulb sign; an axillary or scapular Y view is essential.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: A Colles fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with:
options: Dorsal displacement and angulation producing a dinner-fork deformity
questions.concept: Colles fracture follows a fall on the outstretched hand in an osteoporotic patient, with dorsal tilt, dorsal shift, radial shift and supination. A Smith fracture is the volar-displaced reverse injury.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand suggests:
options: Scaphoid fracture, which is often not visible on the initial radiograph
questions.concept: Because of the risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, a clinically suspected scaphoid fracture is immobilised in a scaphoid cast and re-imaged at 10 to 14 days, or assessed by MRI or CT.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: The nerve most commonly injured in a fracture of the shaft of the humerus is:
questions.concept: The radial nerve lies in the spiral groove against the humerus and is injured in about 10% of shaft fractures. Most are neuropraxias recovering spontaneously, so initial management is conservative with a splint.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a child most commonly injures:
options: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve
questions.concept: The extension-type fracture displaces posteriorly, stretching the median nerve and brachial artery. Loss of the OK sign indicates anterior interosseous palsy, and vascular compromise with Volkmann contracture is the feared complication.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Fractures in Children

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: A Monteggia fracture-dislocation consists of:
options: Fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head
Fracture of the distal radius with distal radioulnar dislocation
questions.concept: Monteggia is ulnar fracture with radial head dislocation; Galeazzi is radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption. In any single forearm bone fracture the joints above and below must be imaged.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes sensory loss over:
options: The lateral three and a half digits, sparing the thenar eminence
The medial one and a half digits
questions.concept: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum, so thenar skin sensation is spared - the key sign distinguishing carpal tunnel compression from a proximal median nerve lesion.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Peripheral Nerve Lesions

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Injury to the ulnar nerve at the elbow produces:
options: Claw hand that is less deforming than a distal lesion, due to the ulnar paradox
questions.concept: A proximal lesion also paralyses flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers, so those fingers cannot flex at the DIP joints and the claw is less marked - the ulnar paradox.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Peripheral Nerve Lesions

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Upper limb injuries: shoulder, humerus, elbow, wrist
questions.stem: Recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation is associated with:
options: A Bankart lesion of the anteroinferior labrum and a Hill-Sachs defect of the humeral head
questions.concept: Detachment of the anteroinferior labrum with capsular stripping predisposes to recurrence, and impaction of the posterolateral humeral head against the glenoid rim creates the Hill-Sachs defect. Arthroscopic Bankart repair is the treatment.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Upper Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: A patient with a shortened, adducted and internally rotated lower limb after a dashboard injury has:
questions.concept: Posterior dislocation accounts for about 90% of hip dislocations and is an orthopaedic emergency; reduction within 6 hours minimises avascular necrosis. Sciatic nerve injury occurs in about 10%.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: A fracture of the neck of femur classically presents with the limb:
questions.concept: External rotation distinguishes it from posterior hip dislocation which is internally rotated. Intracapsular fractures risk avascular necrosis and non-union because the retinacular blood supply is disrupted.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: In an elderly patient with a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture, the treatment of choice is:
questions.concept: Displaced intracapsular fractures in the elderly have high rates of avascular necrosis and non-union after fixation, so replacement allows immediate weight-bearing. Fixation is preferred in the young to preserve the native head.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: The most immediately life-threatening complication of an unstable pelvic fracture is:
questions.concept: The pelvis can conceal several litres of blood from the presacral venous plexus and cancellous bone. A pelvic binder, resuscitation and angiographic embolisation or packing take priority over definitive fixation.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Pelvic Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weakness of:
options: The hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) or their nerve supply
questions.concept: When standing on the affected leg the opposite hemipelvis drops. Causes include superior gluteal nerve palsy, hip dislocation, femoral neck fracture and any condition altering the abductor lever arm.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Examination of the Hip

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: The commonest mechanism of ankle injury producing a lateral malleolar fracture is:
questions.concept: The Weber classification relates the fibular fracture to the syndesmosis: Weber A below, B at, and C above the level, with C implying syndesmotic disruption needing fixation. Ottawa ankle rules guide the need for radiography.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: The unhappy triad of knee injury consists of:
options: Anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus injury
questions.concept: A valgus force with external rotation on a planted foot injures all three structures. The anterior drawer and Lachman tests assess the ACL, and McMurray test the menisci.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Knee Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: A fracture of the shaft of the femur in an adult may cause hypovolaemic shock because it can lose:
options: One to one and a half litres of blood
questions.concept: Closed femoral shaft fractures conceal substantial blood loss, and bilateral fractures or associated pelvic injury can cause profound shock. Early splinting reduces bleeding and pain.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: Common peroneal nerve injury at the neck of the fibula produces:
options: Foot drop with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot
questions.concept: The nerve is superficial at the fibular neck, vulnerable to fractures, tight casts and prolonged squatting. Loss of dorsiflexion and eversion gives a high-stepping gait; the sole is spared as it is supplied by the tibial nerve.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Peripheral Nerve Lesions

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Lower limb & pelvic injuries; hip dislocation
questions.stem: In a suspected femoral neck fracture with normal radiographs, the next investigation is:
questions.concept: MRI detects occult fractures within hours with the highest sensitivity, avoiding the delay of repeat films or the reduced early sensitivity of bone scanning - important as delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes in the elderly.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Lower Limb Injuries

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: The commonest level of lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse is:
questions.concept: The lower lumbar levels bear the greatest mechanical load. A posterolateral L4-5 prolapse compresses the L5 root causing weak great toe dorsiflexion, and L5-S1 compresses S1 with a reduced ankle jerk.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Cauda equina syndrome is an emergency indicated by:
options: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction and bilateral leg weakness
questions.concept: Urinary retention with overflow incontinence and perianal numbness demand urgent MRI and decompression within 24 to 48 hours; delay causes permanent sphincter dysfunction and is a common source of litigation.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: The straight leg raising (Lasegue) test is positive in:
options: Lumbar disc prolapse with nerve root tension
questions.concept: Pain radiating below the knee between 30 and 70 degrees of elevation indicates root irritation, and the crossed straight leg raise is more specific though less sensitive for a large central prolapse.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: The commonest site of tuberculosis of the spine (Pott disease) is:
options: The thoracolumbar junction, beginning in the paradiscal region
questions.concept: Paradiscal involvement destroys the disc and adjacent vertebral bodies producing anterior wedging with kyphosis (gibbus) and a cold abscess. Disc destruction distinguishes it from metastasis, which spares the disc.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Paraplegia complicating spinal tuberculosis is most often due to:
options: Inflammatory oedema, abscess or granulation tissue compressing the cord, which is largely reversible with treatment
questions.concept: Early-onset paraplegia during active disease is usually from compressive inflammatory tissue and responds to antitubercular therapy with or without decompression, whereas late-onset paraplegia from fibrosis or bony ridge has a poorer prognosis.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is assessed radiologically by:
options: The Cobb angle on a standing full-spine radiograph
questions.concept: Curves under 20 degrees are observed, 20 to 40 degrees braced in a skeletally immature patient, and above 45 to 50 degrees considered for fusion. The Adams forward bend test with a rib hump is the clinical screen.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Spinal shock after acute cord injury is characterised by:
options: Transient flaccid areflexic paralysis with loss of the bulbocavernosus reflex
questions.concept: Neurological assessment is unreliable until spinal shock resolves, marked by return of the bulbocavernosus reflex within 24 to 48 hours; only then can a complete injury be confidently diagnosed.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Neurogenic claudication of lumbar canal stenosis is distinguished from vascular claudication by:
options: Relief on sitting or bending forward, with preserved peripheral pulses
questions.concept: Flexion increases canal diameter, so patients report relief on stooping and can cycle further than they can walk. Vascular claudication is relieved simply by stopping, with diminished pulses and a reduced ABPI.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: The most important initial step in managing a suspected cervical spine injury at the scene is:
options: Immobilisation of the whole spine with attention to airway and breathing
questions.concept: Neutral in-line immobilisation prevents secondary neurological injury during airway management and transfer. Routine high-dose steroids are no longer recommended because of harm outweighing benefit.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Spine injury, disc prolapse & spinal deformity
questions.stem: Spondylolisthesis refers to:
options: Forward slipping of one vertebra over the one below
questions.concept: Most commonly at L5 over S1 from a pars interarticularis defect, graded by Meyerding into four quarters of slip. It causes back pain with a step on palpation and may compress nerve roots.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Spine
